cards.front: Why does a body that grows without changing shape have more trouble supplying its middle by diffusion?
cards.back: Its middle ends up farther from its outer surface, and diffusion time grows with the square of that distance.
cards.quote: When a body grows without changing shape, its middle ends up farther from its outer surface, and diffusion time grows with the square of that distance.

cards.front: In a simple model of a solid ball of tissue fed from air at its surface, oxygen runs out at the centre once the radius passes about {{c1::1.5 mm}} for slow tissue.
cards.back: For busy tissue the limit is a few tenths of a millimetre; other shapes give other limits.
cards.quote: oxygen runs out at the centre once the radius passes about 1.5 mm for slow tissue, or a few tenths of a millimetre for busy tissue

cards.front: Name three general ways large bodies get oxygen past the diffusion limit.
cards.back: Stay thin, add internal exchange surfaces, or move fluid in bulk (pumped blood, air or sap), leaving diffusion only the last few micrometres.
cards.quote: So bodies stay thin, add internal exchange surfaces, or move fluid in bulk (bulk flow: pumped blood, air or sap), leaving diffusion only the last few micrometres.

cards.front: For an ideal cube of side s, the surface-area-to-volume ratio is {{c1::6/s}}.
cards.back: Area 6s² (six square faces) over volume s³.
cards.quote: For an ideal cube of side s, the area is 6s² (six square faces) and the volume s³.
cards.section: A bigger cube has less skin per unit of inside

cards.front: Why does a cube's surface-area-to-volume ratio fall as the cube grows?
cards.back: Area grows as s² but volume as s³; two s's cancel, so 6s²/s³ = 6/s, which falls as the side s rises.
cards.quote: Two s's cancel top and bottom, leaving 1/s, so 6s² / s³ = 6/s.
cards.section: A bigger cube has less skin per unit of inside

cards.front: An ideal cube-shaped cell has sides of 5 um. What is its surface-area-to-volume ratio, and how does it compare with a 10 um cube?
cards.back: Area 6 × 25 = 150 um², volume 125 um³, ratio 150/125 = 1.2 per um (6/s). That is twice the 10 um cube's 0.6 per um.
cards.quote: For a cube of side 10 um: 6/10 = 0.6 per um.
cards.section: A bigger cube has less skin per unit of inside

cards.front: For a sphere of radius r, the surface-area-to-volume ratio is {{c1::3/r}}.
cards.back: 4πr² / (4/3 πr³): π cancels, 4 divided by 4/3 is 3, and r² over r³ leaves 1/r.
cards.quote: For a sphere of radius r, surface area over volume is 4πr² / (4/3 πr³) = 3/r.
cards.section: The sphere's ratio, step by step

cards.front: Compare the surface-area-to-volume ratios of spherical cells of radius 5 um and 25 um.
cards.back: Ratio = 3/r. r = 5 um: 0.6 per um. r = 25 um: 0.12 per um. Five times the radius gives one fifth the ratio.
cards.quote: A sphere of radius r gives 3/r (Going deeper).
cards.section: A bigger cube has less skin per unit of inside

cards.front: For a small molecule in water, the diffusion coefficient D is about {{c1::1,000 um² per s}}.
cards.quote: For a small molecule in water, D is about 1,000 um² per s.
cards.section: Diffusion: fast over micrometres, slow over centimetres

cards.front: In a simple model of free diffusion along one direction, the typical time to spread a distance L is t = {{c1::L² / 2D}}.
cards.back: The mean squared distance travelled in time t is 2Dt; its square root is the typical distance L.
cards.quote: In a simple model of free diffusion along one direction, the mean squared distance travelled in time t is 2Dt; its square root is the typical distance L.
cards.section: Diffusion: fast over micrometres, slow over centimetres

cards.front: Why is diffusion fast over micrometres but slow over centimetres?
cards.back: In a simple free-diffusion model, typical time grows with the square of distance (t = L²/2D), so ten times the distance takes a hundred times as long.
cards.quote: and diffusion time grows with the square of that distance

cards.front: Using t = L²/2D with D = 1,000 um² per s, about how long does a small molecule take to diffuse 1 mm?
cards.back: L = 1,000 um, so L² = 1,000,000 um²; 2D = 2,000 um² per s. t = 1,000,000 / 2,000 = 500 s, a little over 8 minutes.
cards.quote: t = 1,000,000 / 2,000 = 500 s, a little over 8 minutes.
cards.section: Diffusion: fast over micrometres, slow over centimetres

cards.front: With D = 1,000 um² per s and t = L²/2D, estimate the typical time for a small molecule to diffuse 10 um, and then 2 mm.
cards.quote: Units: um² divided by um² per s leaves seconds.
cards.section: Diffusion: fast over micrometres, slow over centimetres

cards.front: What does the time from t = L²/2D measure, and what does it not measure?
cards.back: A typical spread along one coordinate. Not the time to fill a cell or the first arrival: some molecules arrive sooner, and evening out a whole region takes longer.
cards.quote: The formula gives a typical spread along one coordinate, not the time to fill a cell or the first arrival
cards.section: What t = L² / 2D does and does not measure

cards.front: In the idealized solid-ball model of oxygen supply, how does the largest radius depend on the tissue's rate of oxygen use?
cards.back: It goes as one over the square root of the rate, so tenfold faster use (0.3 to 3.0 mL O₂ per g per hour) cuts reach only about threefold.
cards.quote: Depth goes as one over the square root of the rate of use, so tenfold faster use (0.3 to 3.0) cuts reach only about threefold.
cards.section: How deep can diffusion reach?

cards.front: In the idealized solid-ball model, tissue using 0.05 mL O₂ per g per hour can be supplied to a radius of 1.45 mm. Estimate the limit for tissue using 0.2 mL O₂ per g per hour.
cards.back: Reach goes as 1/√(rate). The rate is 4 times higher, so reach is 1/√4 = 1/2 as large: about 0.73 mm.
cards.quote: Largest radius of a solid ball whose centre still gets oxygen
cards.section: How deep can diffusion reach?

cards.front: Planarians are flattened and take oxygen in by diffusion through two faces. In the same idealized model, is a sheet's largest half-thickness bigger or smaller than a ball's largest radius, and how does flattening help?
cards.back: Smaller, by about 1.7-fold (√3) at every rate. Flattening does not allow thicker tissue; it works because length and width can grow while thickness stays under the limit.
cards.quote: Flattening does not allow thicker tissue; it works because length and width can grow while thickness stays under the limit.
cards.section: How deep can diffusion reach?

cards.front: Give an animal and a plant example of flattening as an answer to the surface problem.
cards.back: Animal: a planarian (flatworm). Plant: the blade, or lamina, of a typical eudicot leaf, a wide, thin sheet.
cards.quote: a typical eudicot leaf (a broad-leaved flowering plant, such as a bean) is a wide, thin sheet in which no cell is far from the surface
cards.section: Four answers in two kingdoms

cards.front: Give an animal and a plant example of folding an exchange surface inward.
cards.back: Animal: the mammalian lung's alveoli, a vast number of small air sacs. Plant: leaf mesophyll, the photosynthetic tissue, full of air spaces.
cards.quote: The mammalian lung folds its exchange surface into a vast number of small air sacs, the alveoli.
cards.section: Four answers in two kingdoms

cards.front: Why does gas exchange in the mammalian lung depend on surface area divided by barrier thickness?
cards.back: More area gives more surface to cross, and a thin barrier is a short diffusion distance.
cards.why: Diffusion time rises with the square of distance, so thinning the barrier speeds exchange sharply.
cards.quote: Exchange depends on that area divided by the barrier's thickness, because a thin barrier is a short diffusion distance.
cards.section: Four answers in two kingdoms

cards.front: Barley leaves have 21.3 mm² of exposed mesophyll surface per mm² of leaf area. What does the number mean, and what are its units?
cards.back: The inside surface is about 21 times the leaf's one-face area. Area over area has no units, unlike a surface-area-to-volume ratio in per um.
cards.quote: Area over area has no units: the inside surface is fifteen to twenty times the leaf's one-face area, unlike the cube's ratio in per um.
cards.section: Four answers in two kingdoms

cards.front: Give an animal and a plant example of branching for supply or exchange.
cards.back: Animal: mammalian airways, dividing about 23 times from trachea to alveolar sacs in the standard adult human model. Plant: leaf veins branching from the midrib into finer veins.
cards.quote: The airways of the mammalian lung divide about 23 times in the standard textbook model of the adult human, from the trachea to the alveolar sacs.
cards.section: Four answers in two kingdoms

cards.front: Why do dense fine veins help a eudicot leaf?
cards.back: They shorten the path water must take from the xylem, through living tissue, to where it evaporates.
cards.quote: dense fine veins shorten the path water must take from the xylem, through living tissue, to where it evaporates
cards.section: Four answers in two kingdoms

cards.front: What is bulk flow? Give three examples in organisms.
cards.back: Movement of a whole fluid, and everything in it, by a pressure difference or by motors. Examples: breathing, blood circulation, sap in phloem.
cards.quote: Bulk flow moves a whole fluid, and everything in it, by a pressure difference or by motors.
cards.section: Four answers in two kingdoms

cards.front: A student says that because mammals pump air and blood by bulk flow, oxygen reaches the blood without diffusion. What is wrong?
cards.back: Bulk flow never removes diffusion. In the finest airways transport shifts toward diffusion, and oxygen crosses the alveolar wall into the blood by diffusion, not active transport.
cards.quote: In the mammalian lung, transport shifts from bulk airflow toward diffusion in the finest branches, and oxygen crosses the alveolar wall into the blood by diffusion, not by active transport.
cards.section: Four answers in two kingdoms

cards.front: In giant cells of the alga Chara, cytoplasm streams at up to about 100 um per s (maximum). Compare the time to move a small molecule 1 mm by streaming and by diffusion (D = 1,000 um² per s).
cards.back: Streaming at the maximum speed: 1,000 um / 100 um per s = 10 s. Diffusion: t = L²/2D = 1,000,000 / 2,000 = 500 s. Over 1 mm, bulk flow is about 50 times faster at most.
cards.why: Bulk flow time rises in step with distance; diffusion time rises with its square.
cards.quote: Even single cells use it: in the giant cells of the alga Chara, motors drive the cytoplasm round at up to about 100 um per s.
cards.section: Four answers in two kingdoms

cards.front: What is basal metabolic rate?
cards.back: The rate of energy use of an adult endotherm (mammal or bird) at rest, fasted, and at a temperature where it spends nothing extra on heating or cooling.
cards.quote: basal metabolic rate is that rate in an adult endotherm (an animal that keeps itself warm with its own heat: mammals and birds) at rest
cards.section: Body mass and metabolism: Rubner, Kleiber and the debate

cards.front: What did Rubner's 1883 "surface law" in dogs report, and what did it not show?
cards.back: Heat roughly constant per unit of estimated body surface. It ruled out simple proportionality to mass in those dogs, but did not show that surface heat loss is the cause in other animals.
cards.quote: It ruled out simple proportionality in these dogs; it did not show that surface heat loss is the cause in other animals.
cards.section: Body mass and metabolism: Rubner, Kleiber and the debate

cards.front: For bodies of one shape and one density, why does outer surface grow as mass to the power 2/3?
cards.back: Surface grows as length² and mass as length³, so surface grows as mass^(2/3).
cards.quote: surface grows as length², mass as length³, so surface grows as mass to the power 2/3
cards.section: Body mass and metabolism: Rubner, Kleiber and the debate

cards.front: Metabolic rate = a × M^b with b = 0.75. By how much does the total rate rise for an animal ten times heavier?
cards.back: 10^0.75 ≈ 5.6 times, not ten.
cards.quote: the rate goes up by 10^(0.75), about 5.6 times, not ten
cards.section: Body mass and metabolism: Rubner, Kleiber and the debate

cards.front: If metabolic rate = a × M^b with b = 0.75, why does rate per kilogram fall as body mass rises?
cards.back: Rate per kg = a × M^b / M = a × M^(b − 1). With b = 0.75 the exponent is −0.25, a negative power, so it falls as M rises.
cards.quote: With b = 0.75 the exponent is −0.25, a negative power, so rate per kilogram falls as M rises.
cards.section: Body mass and metabolism: Rubner, Kleiber and the debate

cards.front: Two related mammals fit metabolic rate = a × M^0.75 with the same a. One is 16 times heavier. Predict its total rate and its rate per kilogram relative to the smaller one.
cards.back: Total: 16^0.75 = 8 times. Per kg: 16^(−0.25) = 1/2, the same as 8/16.
cards.quote: For rate per kilogram, divide the total by M: rate per kg = a × M^b / M.
cards.section: Body mass and metabolism: Rubner, Kleiber and the debate

cards.front: A 30 g mouse and a 70 kg human. How many times the human's rate per kilogram does the mouse have with b = 3/4, and with b = 2/3?
cards.back: Ratio = (M_human / M_mouse)^(1 − b), mass ratio 70 / 0.03 ≈ 2,333. b = 3/4: 2,333^(1/4) ≈ 7. b = 2/3: 2,333^(1/3) ≈ 13. The exponent alone nearly doubles the difference.
cards.quote: The exponent alone nearly doubles the predicted difference.
cards.section: Body mass and metabolism: Rubner, Kleiber and the debate

cards.front: What mammalian metabolic exponent did White and Seymour (2003) find once body temperature and digestive state were controlled?
cards.back: Near 2/3, not the 3/4 of Kleiber's fit.
cards.why: The fitted exponent depends on how and under what conditions rates are measured.
cards.quote: White and Seymour (2003) found a mammalian exponent near 2/3 once body temperature and digestive state were controlled.
cards.section: Body mass and metabolism: Rubner, Kleiber and the debate

cards.front: What does the fitted metabolic scaling exponent b depend on, and is its cause settled?
cards.back: The group, the state (basal, field or maximal), temperature and method. No explanation of it is settled.
cards.quote: The exponent depends on the group, the state (basal, field or maximal), temperature and method, and no explanation of it is settled.
cards.section: Body mass and metabolism: Rubner, Kleiber and the debate

cards.front: Across 40 rodent species, log basal metabolic rate against log body mass has a slope of 0.70. Predict the change in total rate for a 100-fold rise in mass.
cards.back: 100^0.70 = 10^1.4 ≈ 25 times the total rate.
cards.quote: Within rodents, a 100-fold rise in mass predicts about 100^(0.70), roughly 25 times the total rate
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Log-log slopes of metabolic rate against mass are 0.70 within rodents and 0.68 within birds, but 0.76 when these are pooled with shrews and whales. Why can the pooled slope differ from both?
cards.back: Pooling stretches the mass range, and if the groups differ in their constant a, the line through all of them can be steeper or shallower than within any one group. It is a different quantity.
cards.quote: if the groups differ in their constant a, the line through all of them can be steeper or shallower than the line within any one group
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why can ordinary and phylogenetic regression give different metabolic scaling slopes from the same species data?
cards.back: Related species are not independent points; allowing for shared ancestry can change the estimated slope.
cards.quote: Related species are not independent points, so a phylogenetic regression may give a different slope from an ordinary one
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A pooled metabolic scaling slope near 3/4 matches a vascular branching-network model. Does that confirm the model? What test would?
cards.back: No. A fitted number cannot confirm a mechanism, since other explanations fit too. A test needs a prediction rival explanations do not share, checked in data collected under the same conditions.
cards.quote: Testing one would need a prediction that rival explanations do not share, checked in data collected under the same conditions.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: On the 3/4 fit, a kilogram of human burns about a seventh of what a kilogram of mouse burns. Could a human-sized body shaped like a mouse live on diffusion through its skin?
cards.back: No. Reach grows only with the square root of the drop in demand, about 2.6-fold (√7), while the body gets about 13 times wider (2,333^(1/3)).
cards.why: Rests on reach going as 1/√(rate of use) and, at one shape, width going as mass^(1/3).
cards.quote: Reach grows only with the square root of the drop in demand.
cards.section: Does a lower rate per kilogram rescue a big body?

cards.front: For bodies of one shape and density, which scaling exponent keeps metabolic demand per unit of outer surface constant, and what does b = 3/4 do instead?
cards.back: b = 2/3, because outer surface grows as mass^(2/3). With b = 3/4, demand per unit surface rises with size, about 1.9-fold from mouse to human.
cards.quote: b = 2/3 would keep demand per unit of outer surface constant with size, and b = 3/4 would raise it about 1.9-fold from mouse to human
cards.section: Does a lower rate per kilogram rescue a big body?

cards.front: Tissue in equilibrium with air holds at most about 0.0045 mL of dissolved O₂ per mL. At a resting human average of 0.2 mL O₂ per g per hour (density 1 g per cm³), how long would that store last?
cards.back: 0.2 / 60 ≈ 0.0033 mL per mL per min. 0.0045 / 0.0033 ≈ 1.3 minutes. Stores barely help.
cards.quote: Tissue in equilibrium with air would hold about 0.0045 mL of dissolved O₂ per mL, an upper bound, lasting about 1.3 minutes at the resting human rate
cards.section: The depth model behind the table

cards.front: In the idealized ball model at one shape, diffusion reach grows as M^((1 − b)/2) while body radius grows as M^(1/3). Show that no b from 2/3 to 1 lets reach keep pace.
cards.back: For b ≥ 2/3, (1 − b)/2 is at most 1/6, half of 1/3 or less, so the radius always outgrows the reach.
cards.why: Assumes constant shape, density, K and P, with tissue demand in step with whole-body rate per kilogram.
cards.quote: Since rate per kilogram goes as M^(b − 1), reach grows as M^((1 − b)/2), against a body radius growing as M^(1/3)
cards.section: The depth model behind the table

cards.front: {{c1::Allometry}} is the study of how a trait changes with body size when it does not change in simple proportion.
cards.quote: Allometry is the study of how a trait changes with body size when it does not change in simple proportion.
cards.section: More on the exponent

cards.front: What does the bacterium Candidatus Thiomargarita magnifica, with cells averaging more than 9,000 um long, show about size limits?
cards.back: The limits are conditional: shape and internal arrangement can push a single cell far beyond the usual size.
cards.quote: shape and internal arrangement can push a single cell far beyond the usual size
cards.section: A limit with exceptions
